source_refs.note: Topic 27.3.1 (PDF 168); an original sketch of the three effects is added. The book's single pH range is reported with a note on pepsin.

blocks.text: The activity of an enzyme is affected mainly by temperature, pH and the concentrations of substrate and enzyme; it can also be affected by other substances such as co-enzymes, activators and inhibitors.

items: Temperature and pH: the temperature and pH that give maximum activity are the optimum temperature and optimum pH. Moving away from these values can deactivate the enzyme (its shape changes). Enzymes in the human body work best at about 37 C; the book gives a pH range of 6.4-6.9, though some enzymes, such as pepsin in the stomach, work best at very different pH values.

Concentration of enzyme and substrate: the rate increases as the enzyme or substrate concentration increases, because more binding sites are used and more enzyme-substrate complex forms. Beyond a certain substrate concentration, however, the rate stops increasing (the book says it can even slow down), because the active sites are already occupied.

blocks.alt: Three sketch graphs of rate. Temperature: rate rises to a peak at the optimum (about 37 C) and then falls. pH: rate rises to a peak at the optimum pH and then falls. Substrate concentration: rate rises quickly and then levels off.
blocks.caption: How temperature, pH and substrate concentration affect enzyme activity (original sketch for this topic).
blocks.long_description: Warming speeds up collisions until the optimum; above it the enzyme's shape is lost and the rate falls steeply. Each enzyme also has an optimum pH. With more substrate the rate rises until nearly every active site is busy, after which extra substrate makes little difference.

blocks.prompt: Why does an enzyme stop working at high temperature?
blocks.explanation: Heat breaks the bonds holding its 3D shape, so the active site changes shape (the enzyme is denatured) and the substrate no longer fits.

items: Optimum temperature (about 37 C in humans) and optimum pH.
More enzyme or substrate: faster, until the active sites are full.
